courses.author: Daniel Kahneman
courses.blurb: The landmark tour of the two systems of the mind — the fast, intuitive one and the slow, deliberate one — and the biases, shortcuts, and illusions their partnership produces. Twelve short audio chapters, each with a 10-question quiz to make the ideas stick.

chapters.concepts: System 1 vs System 2 · cognitive ease · priming (with a replication caution) · halo effect · WYSIATI · substitution

options: Working out seventeen times twenty-four in your head
Reading the anger in someone's voice the instant they speak
Checking a contract clause by clause
Parking a car in an awkwardly tight space
quiz.q: Which of these is System 1 — the fast mind — at work?
quiz.why: Detecting emotion in a voice is automatic, instant, and effortless — the signature of System 1. The others all demand slow, deliberate System 2 effort.

options: It cannot access memories
It only switches on during sleep
It is lazy — it rations effort and usually endorses System 1's suggestions without re-examining them
It processes information more slowly than it arrives
quiz.q: Why does System 2 so often fail to catch System 1's mistakes?
quiz.why: System 2 can check the fast mind's work, but effort is costly, so it typically waves through System 1's draft like a busy editor trusting a reporter.

options: Anchoring
Cognitive ease
Loss aversion
Regression to the mean
quiz.q: The same statement feels more believable printed in crisp, clear type than in a faint, blurry font. This is mainly an effect of:
quiz.why: When processing feels fluent and easy, the fast mind relaxes — and that relaxed feeling gets misread as truth, safety, and quality.

options: Plans always improve with each presentation
Repetition creates familiarity, and familiarity creates ease — which the mind mistakes for merit
Senior people have probably endorsed it by now
Nothing — repeated exposure is a good test of quality
quiz.q: A plan has been presented to your team three times and now feels obviously correct. What should make you suspicious of that feeling?
quiz.why: Ease grows with exposure. A circulating proposal arrives preloaded with fluency and can feel stronger than a better plan seen only once.

options: All priming results are fabricated
Priming proves the environment controls us like puppets
Some famous priming findings replicated poorly, so strong claims deserve caution — though context genuinely does nudge thought
Priming only works with words about money
quiz.q: Which statement about priming is the most accurate, based on the lesson?
quiz.why: The broad idea that recent exposures tilt thinking is reasonable, but several headline priming experiments did not hold up well when other researchers retested them.

options: Substitution
WYSIATI
The halo effect
Anchoring
quiz.q: A candidate's first two minutes in an interview impress you, and everything after sounds strong too. What is most likely happening?
quiz.why: A strong first impression sets a curve for everything that follows — later evidence gets interpreted generously, so the verdict feels objective but was largely reached in the first minutes.

options: What You See Is All There Is
When You Sense It, Act On It
What You Seek Is Always True Inside
Why You Say It Alters The Interpretation
quiz.why: System 1 builds the best story it can from whatever information is in front of it and does not stop to ask what is missing.

options: Framing
Substitution
Priming
The availability cascade
quiz.q: You ask yourself, "Will this startup succeed?" — and notice you actually answered "Do I like this founder?" That swap is called:
quiz.why: Faced with a hard target question, the fast mind quietly substitutes an easier one and reports the easy answer as if it were the hard one.

options: How much evidence was gathered
How coherent the story feels
How experienced the judge is
How long the judge deliberated
quiz.q: According to the lesson, confidence in a judgment mostly tracks:
quiz.why: Confidence measures the smoothness and consistency of the story in your head — not the completeness or accuracy of the evidence behind it.

options: Ducking when a ball flies at your head
Finishing a familiar phrase
Sensing hostility in someone's tone
Checking whether an argument actually makes sense
quiz.q: Which of these is primarily System 2 work?
quiz.why: Deliberately verifying logic is slow, effortful, and optional — exactly the kind of work System 2 does and System 1 skips.
